approved: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Stronger Penalties for Serious Failures) Bill 2014

Melissa Price As I was saying yesterday, the Australian people expect their taxpayer dollars to go towards policy measures that improve our communities and benefit Australia as a whole. In its current form, the Social Security (Administration) Act 1999 fails to meet this expectation and its own objectives to ensure compliance measures are met at all times by those who receive income support. The amendments before the House today will significantly strengthen our employment welfare system and its intention for resources to be used efficiently and effectively. This is part of the Abbott government's overall strategy to build a stronger Australia, and to do this we need a skilled workforce, with everyone who has the ability to work contributing to its growth and prosperity. In the budget, this government outlined key policy measures relating to job seekers including its new Work for the Dole program. The amendments before us today will go hand-in-hand with these policy measures to help young job seekers in particular move out of the welfare system and into gainful employment. This will benefit not only job seekers in the long term but their community and the nation as a whole. Under recent changes, job seekers aged 18-30 who have been unemployed for 12 months or more and receiving taxpayer-funded assistance from a Job Services Australia provider will be required to participate in work for the dole activities for 15 hours per week for six months, unless they are working part time. From 1 July next year, all job seekers aged 18-30 and in receipt of Newstart allowance and Youth Allowance will be required to undertake work for the dole for 25 hours per week when in receipt of payment. These rules will apply to new income support recipients with a full work capacity and who are not in education or a part-time apprenticeship. Catryna Bilyk As I was saying last night, before I had to cease my contribution, the restriction of waivers will disproportionately impact on some of the most vulnerable people in our society. These are the people we should reach out a hand to and support—people with mental illness and people experiencing homeless. They are the people who I am very concerned to hear appear to have been described by Joe Hockey as 'leaners'. This government does not understand the challenges faced by the most vulnerable and disadvantaged people in our community. They are completely out of touch with what goes on out there in the real world, or, even worse, they might understand it but they just do not care. They are quite happy for the most vulnerable unemployed Australians to be the collateral damage in a cruel and heartless scapegoating exercise. It is important for a strong mutual obligation system that we have both the carrot and the stick systems—a system of penalties for failing to comply, accompanied by help and incentives to engage with the employment support system. This is why the waivers are so important. When there is a serious failure, the waivers allow the department to consider individual circumstances and whether applying the penalty would be appropriate. The department can consider whether the job seeker has the capacity to comply with the serious failure requirement and whether applying the penalty would cause them serious financial hardship. Also, the job seeker has an opportunity and an incentive to re-engage with the system and return to actively seeking work. What the Abbott government wants to introduce is a system that is cruel and inflexible. There is no argument from this side of the chamber that people should be penalised in some way if they steadfastly refuse to engage in finding suitable employment, or if they do not bother to make any reasonable effort. Moved the second reading of the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Stronger Penalties for Serious Failures) Bill, noting that in 2012 to 2013 the penalty was waived in 68 per cent of the 1,718 serious failures for refusing a job and in 73 per cent of 25,286 cases of repeated noncompliance, and said the tighter rules would save $20.5 million over five years.

Detailed the Human Rights Committee's ninth report, which examined 21 bills and found eight requiring further scrutiny, and highlighted concerns about the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Bill 2014, which responds to a Federal Court finding that wage assessments for workers with intellectual disability were discriminatory.

Opposed the bill, noting only 1,718 of more than 600,000 Newstart recipients were found to have refused suitable work in 2012 to 2013, that 76 per cent of serious failures involve people under 30, and that non-payment penalties could total up to 11 months without Newstart when combined with the government's proposed six-month waiting period.

Supported the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Stronger Penalties for Serious Failures) Bill, arguing 70 per cent of job seekers accept work when offered while 11 per cent had four or five serious compliance failures in a year, and said the bill removes the ability to have an eight-week non-payment penalty waived for refusing suitable work.

Opposed the bill, recalling that as minister he retained but limited the eight-week penalty because only 752 of 26,879 serious non-compliance cases, just over three per cent, involved refusing a job offer, and warned combined with the proposed six-month waiting period for under-30s, penalties could leave some job seekers without income for up to nine months.

Supported the bill, citing 1,718 serious failures for refusing a job in 2012 to 2013 with 68 per cent waived, and 25,286 failures for repeated non-compliance with 73 per cent waived, while criticising Labor's $900 stimulus payments that mistakenly sent over 16,000 payments worth $14 million overseas and 21,000 payments worth over $18 million to deceased taxpayers.

Argued that the bill would strengthen mutual obligation by penalising job seekers who refuse suitable work or repeatedly fail participation requirements, while excluding people unable to work despite genuine barriers. Said reduced penalty waivers would protect welfare-system integrity and save $20.5 million by 2017-18.
Spoke on the bill and criticised a member for supporting a $1.3 billion extra cost on Australian families and then making a speech he said demonised young people.

Argued that the bill was a fair application of mutual obligation, requiring job seekers to accept suitable work or face an eight-week non-payment period while preserving exemptions for special circumstances. Cited employment programs, penalties and incentives including the Tasmanian Jobs Programme and Restart subsidy.

Argued that the bill cruelly targeted vulnerable people by replacing support and flexibility with harsher penalties. Criticised relaxed 457 visa rules, cuts to training and youth programs, and said people with mental illness, homelessness, family violence or other barriers could lose essential payments.

Argued that welfare recipients should meet obligations to taxpayers and that repeated noncompliance should have consequences. Supported mandatory eight-week non-payment periods with one waiver for exceptional circumstances, and outlined employment incentives including the Job Commitment Bonus, relocation assistance and Restart.

Argued that welfare policy should maximise workforce participation and provide opportunity, while supporting penalties for serious failures to meet job-seeking obligations. Supported mandatory consequences for refusing suitable work and persistent noncompliance, with consideration for health, parenting and other exceptional circumstances.

Opposed the bill as punitive legislation that removed the ability to waive an eight-week penalty for refusing suitable work and limited waivers for persistent noncompliance. Argued that vulnerable job seekers needed training, work experience and support, citing unemployment at six per cent and youth unemployment at 13.1 per cent.

Supported the bill's changes to job seeker compliance, including an eight-week non-payment period for refusing suitable work and a once-only waiver for persistent noncompliance. Reported Darwin's unemployment rate at 3.9 per cent and participation rate at 75.7 per cent, and promoted Northern Territory employment opportunities.

Supported the Social Security Legislation Amendment (Stronger Penalties for Serious Failures) Bill 2014, saying it would protect the integrity and sustainability of social security by enforcing consequences for people who refused suitable work or were persistently and wilfully noncompliant. Said the existing eight-week non-payment period would apply while protections for vulnerable job seekers and people with reasonable excuses remained.

Reported that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Human Rights considered four bills scheduled for debate from 1 September 2014, finding one compatible with human rights and deferring the other three, including the Business Services Wage Assessment Tool Payment Scheme Bill 2014.
